domains.support: Randomization used the 'Demo program' but allocation concealment method is not described. Baseline demographics were balanced (p>0.05) supporting adequate randomization.

Blinding status is unclear; intervention films were administered by an ENT specialist. 8 participants dropped out mid-study (5 early recovery, 3 used local steroids), suggesting protocol deviations occurred.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL DATA QUALITY ISSUES: (1) Table 5 (HRQOL Parameters Before and After Treatment) reports data ONLY for the insulin/intervention group — no placebo arm data is presented in this table, making between-group effect size calculation impossible for post-treatment comparisons. The p-values reported in Table 5 appear to be within-group pre-vs-post comparisons for the insulin arm only, not between-group comparisons. (2) TDI olfactory score data (primary endpoint from the prior publication, ref 12) is referenced but not reported quantitatively in this paper — only categorical baseline TDI distribution is shown in Table 3. Per-arm means and SDs for TDI are absent. (3) Figure 2 shows consequences of smell loss before and after 4 weeks for both groups, but numeric values are only in the figure (not extractable as text). (4) The n_randomized per arm is not reported — only 48 enrolled total and 20 per arm completed. It is unclear how the 8 dropouts were distributed between arms. (5) The paper does not report control group post-treatment outcomes in tabular form, severely limiting meta-analytic utility. (6) Perception of fire/smoke and emotional satisfaction outcomes shown in Figure 2 could not be extracted as values appear only in figure bars. Omitted figure-only outcomes: perception of fire/smoke, emotional satisfaction (pre/post for both groups from Figure 2).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested intranasal insulin fast-dissolving films (40 IU, three times per week) against placebo films in 40 post-COVID-19 adults with anosmia lasting more than two months. After four weeks, the insulin group showed statistically significant improvements across all key quality-of-life measures compared to baseline, including problems with eating (90% affected before treatment vs. 0% after), personal hygiene difficulties (85% vs. 0%), reduced work ability (75% vs. 0%), and cooking difficulties (50% vs. 0%), all at p<0.0001. The trial was small (20 patients per arm), single-centre, and conducted in Egypt, limiting generalisability; no safety concerns were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: All primary HRQoL outcomes showed pre-to-post improvement in the insulin group significant at p<0.0001 (e.g. eating problems: 90% before vs. 0% after; work reduction: 75% vs. 0%); no between-group statistical comparison table was reported for post-treatment scores.

summary: This prospective single-center cohort study from Italy followed 83 COVID-19 patients with chemosensory dysfunction over 4 years using Sniffin' Sticks psychophysical testing and self-reported VAS measures. summary: This non-randomized prospective study compared olfactory outcomes in 45 long COVID patients (anosmia/hyposmia ≥180 days post-infection) treated with um-PEA-LUT plus olfactory training for 3 months versus 40 MS patients on standard DMTs, using Sniffin' Sticks TDI scoring. At baseline, COVID-19 patients had markedly lower TDI scores (mean 12.6±5.1, mostly anosmic) versus MS patients (mean 33.5±4.9, mostly normosmic); after 3 months, 71.2% of COVID-19 patients recovered normal/borderline-normal olfaction (TDI 34.3±4.6), while MS patients showed stable olfactory function with no significant T0-T1 change. MS patients treated with IFN-beta 1a or glatiramer acetate had no olfactory dysfunction at follow-up (p=0.02 vs. other DMTs), suggesting a hypothesis-generating rationale for investigating DMT in refractory post-COVID olfactory loss.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is primarily a hypothesis-generating comparative study, not an RCT; the two arms have different underlying diseases making between-group effect sizes difficult to interpret clinically. Overall T1 TDI means for the full long COVID arm are not reported as a single summary statistic — they are split into 'recovered' (n=32, TDI 34.3±4.6) and 'non-recovered' (n=13, TDI 18.5±8.1) subgroups. MS arm T1 data are only reported for the 10 patients with residual olfactory impairment. Several figures (Figures 1–4) show estimation plots with additional data that could not be extracted numerically from the text. The arm_id=2 (MS) uses multiple different DMTs — heterogeneous comparator. Table rendering in the source appeared garbled (merged cells in DMT treatment table); patient counts per DMT were: Fingolimod 8, Teriflunomide 7, Ocrelizumab 4, Cladribine 3, Dimethylfumarate 6, IFN-beta 1a Avonex 1, Natalizumab 4, IFN-beta 1a Plegridy 3, Glatiramer Acetate 2 (total=38, slight discrepancy with n=40 analyzed — likely 2 counted differently or table formatting issue). summary: This single-arm prospective study evaluated 12 months of olfactory training (OT) using four classical odors twice daily in 83 patients with persistent olfactory dysfunction (anosmia or cacosmia) at least 2 months after confirmed COVID-19 infection. Mean olfactory VAS scores improved significantly from 0 at baseline to 6.95±2.28 at 3 months, 7.59±2.13 at 6 months, and 7.96±1.97 at 12 months (p=0.0001), with 49.3% of patients achieving full recovery (VAS 9-10) and only 1 patient (1.2%) showing no recovery. Recovery rates increased with longer OT duration and did not differ significantly between male and female patients.
